newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: INTERVIEW-Fore sees widespread ATM needs.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Fore sees widespread ATM needs.

text.p: U.S-based networking product company Fore Systems expects demand for its ATM technology to spread from research-based corporations to businesses and on to homes, senior officials said on Monday.
ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) technology allows networks to deliver voice, video and data simultaneously faster and more efficiently.

"Networking had been for specialists. With the Web you've seen in business (that) suddenly networks have become accessible to more forms. The development then takes it actually to be a home-type technology," David Drury, Fore's senior director of marketing-corporate communications, told Reuters.

With ATM, the man-in-the-street is able to tap into networks like the Internet for fast response to social, educational and domestic lifestyle services from healthcare to distance learning to baby-sitting.
Drury said the widespread demand was created by changes happening in desktop computing.

"All of this is what services do -- we deliver to the average user on the desktop. If you have a look at what Intel and Microsoft are doing, the next generation of desktop processors will have multimedia extensions," he said.
The arrival of DVD (digital video disc) also offers huge storage capacity for multimedia applications.
"We need a network that can support the applications," Drury said.
While the push towards ATM was similar for Asia and the U.S., Fore was seeing the fastest growth in Asia because it was expanding its operations here, he said.
Greg Knowles, Fore's business development manager for Asia/Pacific operations, said another factor was Asian speed in adopting ATM technology.
"There was already a very large installed base in the U.S. and Europe. Here, a lot of the companies have been able to leapfrog some of the existing technologies," said Knowles.

Currently about 25 percent of Fore's revenue comes from Asia. In the financial year ended March 1996, Fore recorded a revenue of US$235.2 million and for the first two quarters of fiscal 1997, it had revenue of about US$181 million.

Drury said Fore was expected to at least mirror the explosive growth rate in Internet usage which is seen rising 10-fold to 300 million users in the next five years from about 30 million users presently. The growth in Asia would be faster initially, he said.

On competition from existing network technology like Fast Ethernet, Drury said the price of a desktop enabled with ATM technology has dropped by a factor of 20 since the introduction of ATM four years ago.
"In terms of providing bandwidth, ATM is now the cheapest technology," he said.
Microsoft's licensing of Fore's ATM for integration with future versions of Windows PC re-enforces ATM as a mainstream technology, he said.
